name: Street style

lead: Street style is fashion that comes from ordinary people on the street rather than from runways or studios. People use it as a reference for putting outfits together, and the appearance payoff is better fit, colour and proportion in everyday clothing.

Wikipedia describes it as often linked to youth culture and big cities, with roots in post-war subcultures and a boost from fashion blogs and Instagram. Research specific to using it for self-improvement is not available; it is a style practice rather than a treatment.

paras: Followers browse street-style photography, blogs and social feeds, collect outfit references, and recreate looks with pieces they own or buy, often adapting for their body shape and climate. Many mix basics such as jeans, sneakers and jackets with one distinctive item.
There are no health risks. The main considerations are cost, chasing quick-turnover trends, and that blogs have been noted for favouring thin, tall and white models.

angle.text: Street style gives concrete outfit references that people adapt to their own wardrobe. Clothes that fit and are well combined change how the body and face are perceived.

lead: Street style is fashion considered to have emerged from the population at large rather than from studios or runways. It is usually associated with youth culture and major cities, centres on individual expression, and lets wearers show several identities at once.[1]

For people trying to improve their appearance, street style serves as a practical reference library: photographed real outfits show how colours, proportions, layers and footwear combine on actual bodies. It overlaps with looksmaxxing's clothing and fit advice, since a well-chosen outfit changes how height, shoulders and build read.

Historically, 20th-century subcultures defined successive street looks: teddy boys and bikers in the 1950s, mods and hippies in the 1960s, punks in the 1970s, goths in the 1980s.[1] In the 2000s fashion blogs and later Instagram made street style a global photographic genre.[1][2]

paras: Wikipedia defines street style as fashion emerging from the general population and linked to youth, cities and individualism over trend-following; wearers use it as a kind of performance of identity.[1]

Street fashion existed earlier but became notable in the 20th century. After World War II, standardization through suburbanization, mass marketing and television may have increased the appeal of alternative styles.[1] New York influences cited include the flapper look of the 1920s and 1930s-40s workwear, and Japanese designers such as Kenzo Takada (1970) and Issey Miyake (1973) arrived in Paris and influenced Western fashion.[1]

Photographer Bill Cunningham of The New York Times treated street photography as a record of what ordinary people wear, saying the best fashion show is on the street.[1] Blogs narrowed the gap between fashion houses, publications and individuals, and Instagram became a main platform for both amateur and professional street-style photographers.[1]

Mainstream brands often borrow street trends. Sportswear and skateboarding have shaped street looks, and skate shoes are worn by non-skaters.[1] The Wikipedia article notes that blogs show more variety in bodies than traditional editorials, though many still favour thinness, height and whiteness.[1] Commentary on the genre includes pieces such as a 2018 look back at how street-style blogs reshaped fashion, shared on Hacker News in 2024.[2]

timeline.event: Subcultures such as teddy boys, mods, punks and goths define successive street looks.[1]
